transcript.text: Hi, my Hotpoint Aquarius dryer is taking forever to dry and the top gets really hot. Model is TCM580GUK if that helps

That sounds like an airflow issue rather than a broken part. When air can't flow freely through the machine, heat builds up (making the top hot) but the moisture stays in the clothes because it isn't being vented out. The most common cause is a blocked lint filter or condenser unit. Even if you think they are clean, fluff can pack into the mesh and block airflow significantly. 1. Unplug the machine for safety.
2. Remove the lint filter from the door opening and rinse it under warm water to remove all fluff. Let it dry completely before putting it back.
3. Shake off excess water and let it drip dry for a few minutes before refitting it securely. Once that is done, try running a normal drying cycle with a moderate load of well-spun laundry. If the machine still gets very hot but takes ages to dry, or if the clothes come out damp, let me know exactly what happens.

Thank you. I unplugged it and took the filter out, and it had a really thick layer of fluff on it, I'll admit I sometimes forget to clean it. I've rinsed it and I'm letting it dry. I should also say I often run the dryer while I'm out at work, if that matters.

Since the lint filter was very blocked, there is probably fluff buildup in the condenser unit as well. On your Hotpoint Aquarius TCM580GUK (a condenser dryer), this unit sits behind a small flap at the bottom front of the door opening. It needs to be removed and rinsed clean just like the lint filter. Once both filters are clean and dry, try a normal drying cycle with a moderate load of well-spun laundry. If you find the condenser was clogged or if the machine still takes ages to dry after cleaning both filters, let me know exactly what happens.
Thanks. I found the condenser unit at the front bottom and it had lint packed on the fins. I've rinsed it and it looks much cleaner now. Is there anything else I should check before I run it again?

Cleaning both the lint filter and the condenser unit should restore proper airflow, which will stop the overheating and allow the dryer to work efficiently again. A quick tip for next time: since you often run it while out at work, try to give the condenser a quick rinse every few weeks if you can. It only takes a minute and stops that thick fluff buildup from happening in the first place. Go ahead and run your cycle when everything is dry.
